title: 90% of Toilets Are Cleaned Wrong (Here's the Right Way)
description:
Your toilet doesn't push anything down. It pulls. There's no pump - water goes into the bowl fast enough to fill the S-bend behind it, the whole thing turns into a siphon, and the toilet drinks itself empty. That gurgle at the end is air breaking the siphon.

Every drop of water that does that comes out of a ring of small holes under the rim, fed by a channel about the width of your finger: dark, wet, warm, never dries out. No brush you have ever owned has been in there. That channel is where the ring in your bowl is made - it isn't born in the bowl, it's delivered down the sides on every flush. Which is why the ring is back three days after you scrub it.

I cleaned toilets for eleven years with the tank lid on. The whole method is in the first ninety seconds.

THE PRINTED CHECKLIST - tape it inside the cabinet door under the sink

THE 20-MINUTE VERSION
1. Shut the valve behind the toilet, down low - clockwise until it stops.
2. Flush and hold the handle down. The bowl empties and stays empty.
3. Squirt 3% hydrogen peroxide up into the holes under the rim, all the way around.
4. Lay 4-5 flat sheets of toilet paper on the ring at the waterline and soak them. The paper is what holds it there - liquid on a vertical wall is gone in six seconds.
5. Two cups of peroxide in the tank while that sits.
6. Twenty minutes. Brush the rim, the ring, the tank walls. Open the valve. Flush twice.

DWELL TIMES
Rim and ring: 20 minutes minimum. Old ring: two hours, or overnight with the lid down. Tank: 1-2 hours, then flush through. Thick film: break it up with the brush, treat it, then treat it again next week - the second treatment is the one that wins.

ONCE A YEAR
- Clear the rim jets: white vinegar and a stiff wire or zip tie into each hole. Bleach and peroxide do NOT dissolve mineral.
- Check the flapper. Soft, slippery, black on your fingers = a $5 part, and the reason it runs at 2 a.m.
- Flip up the seat hinge caps: peroxide and an old toothbrush, thirty seconds.
- The seam where the porcelain meets the floor. That's usually where the smell is.

WEEKLY, 40 SECONDS
Peroxide on a cloth: the wall behind and beside the toilet, the side of the vanity, the flush handle, the underside of the seat, the baseboard. Close the lid before you flush. Rinse the brush in the clean flush water, wedge the handle under the seat to drip dry, and keep peroxide in the bottom of the holder cup.

NO IN-TANK BLUE TABLETS
Kohler puts a sticker inside the tank: in-tank cleaners void the warranty and can destroy parts and cause leaks. Fluidmaster prints it in capitals. And it never reaches the ring anyway - the ring is fed from the rim channel, not the tank water.

SAFETY - please read this part
- NEVER mix bleach with a toilet bowl cleaner. Those thick gels in the angled bottles are acid, and bleach plus acid makes chlorine gas. The common way it happens: clean with the gel, it doesn't look clean enough, pour bleach on top without flushing first.
- NEVER pour bleach into a bowl with urine standing in it. Urine contains ammonia; bleach plus ammonia makes chloramine.
- NEVER mix peroxide and vinegar in a bottle and store it (peracetic acid). Use one, rinse, use the other.
- 3% only, the brown drugstore bottle. Not 35%. It's brown because light turns peroxide into water - a clear spray bottle left on a windowsill is water now.
- A hard raised ring is mineral. Peroxide won't touch it: wet pumice on wet porcelain, and test a hidden spot first on a colored or vintage fixture.
- If the smell survives all of it and is worse in warm weather, that's the wax ring or the subfloor - a pull-and-reset job, not a spray bottle job.
- A guest bath that smells like sewer usually isn't dirty: the trap dried out. Pour a cup of water in there once a month.
